questions.note: Option 2 is long but the only legally sound option.
Art 19(c) incompatibility; objection not opposing entry into force leaves treaty in force between A and B (VCLT Art 20(4)(b)).
Answer turns on self-execution analysis; option 3 is the only careful one.

Option 2 ('Conduct attributable to the state under international law') is cut off: it lists only one element, but the stem asks for two (attribution and breach of an international obligation, ILC Art 2). Other options are plainly wrong.
Option 3 (necessity) is garbled and contradicts Art 25; option 0 (distress) is the clear answer.

Option 0 is the only defensible one (immunity ratione personae ends on leaving office) but does not address the private-vs-official split; option 3 reverses the rule (official acts stay covered by ratione materiae).
Option 1 is a bare hedge ('may be lawful self-defence against armed attack'); option 0 is clearly wrong since T lacked S's request (Nicaragua).
Option 0 is awkwardly worded but is the only choice matching reciprocity.
Option 2 is incomplete: Annex VII arbitration is right for the merits, but immediate release of vessel and crew is Art 292 ITLOS prompt release; option omits that and reads as truncated.
Option 1 reads as truncated ('may have jurisdiction on the basis of territory'); Rome Statute Art 12(2)(a) territorial basis and Art 17 unwilling/unable support it.
Option 1 is cut off after 'passage that does not prejudice peace' (no ending). Correct choice otherwise (UNCLOS Arts 17, 19; Corfu Channel).
Option 2 is very short ('lawful as hot pursuit under Article 111'); Art 111 verified: pursuit may start from EEZ for EEZ-law violations and continue on the high seas if uninterrupted.
Option 0 is hedged ('probably'); Pulp Mills supports the EIA duty for significant transboundary risk.
Option 3 is cut off mid-sentence ('by claim of sovereignty, use'); it omits 'or occupation, or by any other means' from Art II. Still the only correct choice.
